abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: The clinical translation of combined immunocytokine (IC) and immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) is constrained by relapse of advanced malignancies, systemic toxicities, and prohibitive research and synthesis costs. In this study, the circCV-B3 vector is constructed to enable scarless circular RNA (circRNA) engineering. The circILNb, engineered via the circCV-B3 vector, enables co-encoding of interleukin-15 (IL-15) and anti-PD-L1 nanobody (Nb). The circILNb is purified by biotin-avidin purification system (BAPS) and is encapsulated within lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Intratumoral circILNb administration achieves in situ protein expression, achieving local tumor control. Furthermore, dendritic cells (DCs) load circILNb and migrate to tumor-draining lymph node (tdLN), where they prime antigen-specific CD8+ T cell activation, eliciting a robust systemic immune response. These findings highlight the potential of circCV-B3 vector and BAPS as a methodology for circRNA engineering and substantiate circILNb as non-protein-based therapeutic strategy for tumor immunotherapy.

abstract.p: Niu et al. construct the circCV-B3 vector to enable scarless circRNA engineering. Utilizing circCV-B3 vector, they engineer circILNb for co-encoding IL-15 and anti-PD-L1 nanobody. Additionally, they demonstrate circILNb’s potent suppression of both local and distal tumors. The authors also demonstrate the superior antitumor efficacy of circILNb compared to protein-based therapeutics.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Immunotherapies have revolutionized the clinical paradigm of tumor treatment. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) that target PD-1/PD-L1 continue to be approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for monotherapy and combination therapy of tumor.1,2 Nevertheless, the clinical benefits of these approaches in patients with advanced tumor have been limited. In general, advanced tumors exhibit low rates of somatic mutation, contain few infiltrating lymphocytes, and express low levels of PD-L1. These characteristics are indicative of an immunologically “cold” tumor.3,4 A number of immunocytokines (ICs) have been identified as modulators of T cell expansion, survival and function, including interleukin-2 (IL-2), IL-7, IL-12 and IL-15. These are the subject of ongoing investigation in clinical trials, both as monotherapy and in combination with other treatments.5 IC has the potential to transform a cold tumor into a hot tumor. In synergy with ICI, an augmented antitumor response can be produced.6,7 However, its application in the clinic is hindered by numerous technical challenges, safety concerns, pleiotropic effects and the suboptimal efficacy observed in advanced tumor. Despite the development of various strategies to enhance the activity (cytokine-receptor pairs), target (antibody-fusion), or combine therapy, the costly synthetic and product processes, limited durability, and the insufficient anticipated therapeutic efficacy still necessitate improved strategies to harness the potential of IC and ICI combination therapy.8,9

Nanobody (Nb), also known as single-domain antibody, is derived from the variable domain of the heavy chain of the heavy chain-only antibody (VHH) found in camelids.10,11 These unique antibody fragments represent the smallest known antibody molecule of binding antigen, with a mere size of approximately 15 kDa and a length of about 2.5 nanometers. Due to their small size, Nb possesses several advantageous properties for medical applications: (1) high affinity and specificity, (2) high solubility, (3) intra-tissue penetration, and (4) low immunogenicity.12,13 However, there are still some significant limitations, including the short half-life, non-multivalency, and pharmacokinetic issues.14,15 Due to the shortcomings in this regard, many studies have used carriers to express Nb in situ, including bacteria and lentiviruses. However, the advantages of Nb have yet to be fully realized.16,17

Circular RNA (circRNA) is covalently closed, single-stranded RNA. The circRNA is more stable than linear mRNA due to their closed circular structure, which protects them from exonuclease-mediated degradation.18,19 The in vitro transcription (IVT) of translatable circRNA involves four-step process: (1) the design of linear RNA precursor that contain the internal ribosome enter site (IRES), (2) synthesis of linear RNA precursor, (3) circularization reaction, and (4) purification. Of note, circRNA have great potential to become the next generation of RNA-based therapeutic platforms. However, the technology of circRNA synthesis remains immature. On the one hand, the permuted intron-exon (PIE) method, which is widely used due to its simplicity and suitability for high-throughput preparation, imports exogenous auxiliary-exons into circRNA. These scar sequences may affect sequence accuracy and advanced folded RNA structure, and to form resemble double-stranded RNA, which can induce uncontrollable immunogenicity and unwanted side effects.20 On the other hand, inadequate purification will retain some contaminants from synthetic reactions that are highly immunogenic.21 As the traditional methods, RNase R treatment is inadequate in the complete degradation of linear RNA, and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is unable to eliminate linear RNA that possesses a comparable molecular weight.22

In this study, we have refined the PIE strategy to devise circRNA vector, designated circCV-B3. The circCV-B3 vector accommodated insertion of coding sequences (CDSs), enabling to engineer protein-encoding circRNA devoid of scar sequences. Moreover, we have developed a biotin-avidin purification system (BAPS) to enhance the purity of the target circRNA. Based on the circCV-B3 vector, the circILNb has been engineered to co-encode IL-15 and anti-PD-L1 Nb. Following intratumoral (i.t.) injection of lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated circILNb, i.t. circILNb-loaded cells facilitated in situ protein coding while circumventing systemic exposure, concurrently activating pre-existing CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells within the tumor, thereby eliciting potent local antitumor efficacy. Furthermore, i.t. circILNb-loaded dendritic cells (DCs) migrated to tumor-draining lymph node (tdLN) to activate antigen-specific CD8+ T cell responses, thereby initiating a systemic antitumor immune response. The circCV-B3 vector and BAPS enable cost-effective production and high-yield synthesis of circRNA. The engineered circILNb via the circCV-B3 vector provides therapeutic strategy for combined IC and ICI in cold tumors immunotherapy.

sec.title: Construction of circCV-B3 vector and engineering circILNb
sec.p: The ribozymatic method utilizes permuted group I catalytic intron to form PIE chimeras for customized sequence circularization (Figure S1A).23 Specifically, the ligation site of T4td group I catalytic intron can be minimized to E1 (TTGGGT) and E2 (CT), respectively, while maintaining autocatalytic activity (Figure S1B).24 An attempt was made to conceal the ligation site into the nascent circRNA in order to avoid the introduction of exogenous T4td E1E2 sequences. In CVB3 IRES, two segments match E1E2, which is more suitable for masking E1E2.25,26 Mutations 1 and 2 have been conducted, and secondary structure prediction revealed that mutation 1 had a negligible effect on the correct folding of IRES (Figure S1C). Consequently, the CVB3 IRES mutation 1 was selected as the IRES for subsequent vector design. Building upon the PIE, the linear RNA precursor was redesigned with restriction enzyme sites (RESs) downstream of IRES, and subsequently cloned into a plasmid harboring a T7 promoter. This plasmid is designated as the circCV-B3 vector. (Figure 1A). We utilized Sanger sequencing technology confirmed the correct circularization of linear RNA precursor (Figure S1D). Further RNase R enrichment assay demonstrated the existence of circRNA (Figures S1E and S1F). The capillary electrophoresis technology also confirmed the existence of circRNA and verified the circularization efficiency increased to 90% (Figures S1G). RNA secondary structure prediction confirmed the independent and proper folding of each functional element within the circRNA (Figures S1H and S1I).

sec.p: We also design the BAPS method to purify circRNA. The design of the hybridization probe was informed by the sequence of the circRNA ligated site (Figure S2A). The BAPS is utilized to achieve circRNA pull-down (Figure S2B). Probe was found to be effective in the isolation of circRNA, while no products were observed in the presence of oligo dT (Figure S2C). It was established that 10 pmol of probe was optimal for achieving maximum pull-down efficiency (Figure S2D). Consequently, it was observed that an increase in the number of beads led to a corresponding enhancement in the pull-down efficiency (Figure S2E). We employed a combination of RNase R digestion and HPLC purification system as a comparative analysis. The results of this analysis are consistent with those reported in the literature, with the circRNA purity measured at approximately 90%. Conversely, the circRNA purity obtained through BAPS approaches 100%, exhibiting minimal contaminants (Figures S2F and S2G). This finding underscores the high efficiency of BAPS in purifying circRNA.

We next verify the superiority and encoding capacity of circCV-B3 vector. Based on circCV-B3 vector, we engineered the firefly luciferase-expressed circRNA (circLuc) (Figure S3A), along with N1-methylpseudouridine (N1Ψ)-modified mRNA and circRNA synthesized via the conventional PIE method (circRNA-PIE). We found that circCV-B3 achieved 90% circularization efficiency post-circularization reaction, compared to 70% for circRNA-PIE (Figure S3B). Moreover, toward host cell growth, no significant cytotoxicity was observed for any of the exogenous RNAs (Figure S3C). Additionally, we found that circCV-B3 possesses superior protein-coding capability, maintaining high expression abundance within 3 days, whereas mRNA began to decline significantly by day 2 (Figure S3D). Regarding the immunogenicity of exogenous RNA, we found that mRNA, owing to nucleotide modifications, induced low immunogenicity. Conversely, circRNA-PIE exhibited higher immunogenicity due to the scar sequences. In contrast, circCV-B3 demonstrated minimal immunogenicity (Figure S3E). Thus, circRNA engineered via the circCV-B3 vector exhibits superior protein-coding capacity and low immunogenicity.

Furthermore, based on circCV-B3 vector, we engineered circGFPmCherry co-encoding GFP and mCherry with a cleavable 2A linker, to examine the encoding efficiency in one circRNA expressing multiple proteins (Figure S4A). We demonstrated that circGFPmCherry efficiently expressed both proteins correctly while maintaining undiminished coding capacity (Figure S4B). Next, we encapsulated circLuc with LNP using microfluidic technology to identify the biodistribution and persistence of circLuc in vivo. The findings revealed that the i.t. can direct local expression (Figures S4C) and firefly luciferase expression can persist for a duration of up to five days, exhibiting a dose-dependent response (Figure S4D). Thus, circRNA engineered via the circCV-B3 vector possesses the capacity to simultaneously encode two distinct proteins and, following i.t. injection, exhibits sustained i.t. retention and prolonged expression.

The objective of this study is to express IL-15 and Nb using a single circRNA, thereby reducing the complexity and cost of drug synthesis. For IL-15, we engineered its bioactive form, namely the fusion of IL-15 with its co-activating receptor subunit IL-15Rα (circIL). This decision was driven by our finding that IL-15 lacking the IL-15Rα subunit exhibited negligible tumor-inhibitory activity (Figure S5A). By isolating primary murine CD8+ T cells and NK cells, we confirmed the pivotal role of the IL-15Rα subunit in activating the downstream signaling phosphorylated STAT5 (p-STAT5) (Figures S5B–S5D). For Nb, we queried the Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics (RCSB) Protein DataBank (https://www.rcsb.org/) for various candidate anti-PD-L1 Nbs. The Nb candidates were designed as 8AOK, 5JDS, and 5DXW.27,28 (Figure S6A). A human influenza hemagglutinin tag is added to the 3′ end for identification, and an IL-2 secretion peptide is added to the 5′ end of the Nb sequence for driving extracellular secretion (Figure S6B). Consistent molecular weight Nb protein expression was obtained (Figure S6C). Furthermore, a PD-L1 blockade experiment has been devised (Figure S6D), and it has been determined that 5DXW had the strongest ability to block the binding of PD-1 to PD-L1 (Figures S6E and S6F). Consequently, the circ5DXW was selected to engineer circNb. For the circILNb, we utilized a cleavable 2A linker (2A) to connect IL-15 with Nb (Figure 1B). Subsequent examination of the expression of circILNb revealed that, a portion of the 2A remained at the C-terminus of the upstream IL-15, resulting in an increase in its molecular weight (Figure 1C).

To satisfy the requirements for in vivo delivery, microfluidic technology is utilized for the purpose of encapsulating the three circRNAs with LNP. The spherical nanoparticles of LNP-circRNA are confirmed (Figures S7A). The average diameter of LNP-circRNA was measured to be approximately 90 nm (Figures S7B and S7C). The polydispersity index (PDI) of LNP-circRNA was found to be less than 0.2 (Figure S7D). Additionally, it was determined that the encapsulation efficiencies of all LNP-circRNAs were above 98% (Figure S7E). With regard to the storage solution for large-scale prepared LNP-circRNA, it was found that storing at 4°C can maintain the physical stability and encapsulation efficiency for a period of at least one month (Figures S7F–S7H). Therefore, the LNP-circRNA that was synthesized fulfills the criteria for in vivo delivery.

Next, validation was conducted by means of i.t. delivery of both circNb and circILNb, which express the HAtag. HA-tagged Nb has been found to colocalize with PD-L1 in wide areas of the tumor (in yellow), representing the on-target distribution of Nb in the tumor (Figure 1D). Moreover, both leukocytes (CD45+) and tumor cells (CD45−) were loaded with circRNA for in situ protein coding (Figures 1E and 1F). Collectively, circILNb demonstrates robust in vivo expression, meriting further investigation into its therapeutic potential.

sec.title: circILNb enhances advanced tumor repression and overcomes Nb resistance
sec.p: We firstly monitored the in vivo distribution and persistence of the IL-15 encoded by circIL and circILNb. The established B16F10 tumors were treated with a single i.t. injection of 0.5 mg/kg per mouse. The results demonstrated that IL-15 with transient elevation was rapidly cleared from the peripheral blood within 24 h (Figure S8A). Further discoveries revealed that circIL and circILNb exhibit sustained encoding capabilities within the tumor, enabling the production of IL-15 within the tumor that persists for at least 6 days (Figure S8B). This finding prompted us to further examine the toxic side effects of circILNb. Compared to the PBS or circScram (circLuc), circILNb induced no significant increase in spleen weight, further indicating i.t. injection of circILNb can effectively shield IL-15 within the tumor mass (Figure S8C). Consistent with this, multiple systemic toxicity evaluations—including hepatotoxicity markers: alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), circulating inflammatory cytokines (interferon [IFN]-γ and IL-6), and circulating NK cell levels—demonstrated no significant upregulation following circILNb administration (Figures S8D–S8H). Therefore, i.t. injection of circILNb exhibits low systemic toxicity.

In order to select the appropriate dosage for subsequent research, an investigation was first conducted into the inhibitory effects of different dosages of the circRNA on advanced tumors (Figure S9A). The results revealed that all circRNAs exhibited a dose-dependent inhibitory effect on tumor growth. Of particular note was the finding that circILNb demonstrated the most significant inhibitory effects on tumor growth, accompanied by a substantial prolongation of survival time in mice, even at a medium dosage of 0.5 mg/kg. Conversely, a low dosage of circNb exhibited no significant effect (Figures S9B, S9C, S9E, S9F, S9H, and S9I). Furthermore, both circIL and circILNb significantly reduced body weight after injection (Figures S9D and S9J). Notably, the short half-life of Nb ensures that even high-dose administration exerts minimal impact on body weight (Figure S9G). The aforementioned results revealed that a dosage of 0.5 mg/kg can elicit optimal tumor inhibitory effects without causing significant toxicity to mice.

Next, the therapeutic potential of circIL, circNb, and circILNb on advanced tumor was evaluated. Four typical cold tumor models were selected, namely melanoma (B16F10), prostate cancer (RM-1), breast cancer (4T1), and colorectal cancer (CT26) (Figure 2A). In all four tumor models, circNb had the lowest effect on tumor repression and protection of mice. Conversely, circILNb significantly enhanced tumor inhibition and increases survival for all advanced tumor-bearing mice, particularly in the B16F10 model (Figures 2B–2I). The administration of circRNA therapeutics did not result in any significant alterations in body weight in the mice (Figures S10A–S10E). In summary, the administration of 0.5 mg/kg of circILNb has been demonstrated to elicit a substantial tumor-inhibiting effect on advanced cold tumors.

sec.title: circILNb induces expansion and activation of pre-existing CD8+ T cells and NK cells
sec.p: To investigate whether circILNb could induce expansion and activation of different tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs), TILs were analyzed after the second treatment (Figure 3A). A significant increase in the proportion of CD45+ cells was observed, particularly in the circILNb group (Figure S11A). However, no significant changes in the proportion of CD4+ cells were detected (Figure S11B), while the proportion of immunosuppressive CD4+ Foxp3+ Treg cells was significantly decreased under circIL or circILNb treatment (Figure S11C). Conversely, the proportion of toxicity CD8+ T cells was significantly promoted, particularly in the case of circILNb treatment (Figure 3B). This phenomenon resulted in a notable increase in the ratio of CD8+ cells to Treg cells (Figure S11D). NK cells were found to be upregulated following circILNb treatment. Additionally, a substantial upregulation in the proportion of natural killer T cell (NKT) was observed following treatment with circIL and circILNb (Figure 3C). Thus, circILNb elicited a substantial expansion of both the NK and CD8+ T cell populations within the tumor.

sec.p: To further validate the crucial roles of TILs under circILNb therapy, the depletion of CD4+ T, CD8+ T, or NK cells was conducted in B16F10 tumor-bearing mice. CD4+ cells exerted minimal influence on circILNb-mediated tumor repression. Conversely, depletion of CD8+ cells or NK cells significantly diminished the antitumor efficacy (Figures S12A and S12B). Notably, co-depletion of CD8+ T cells and NK cells completely abrogated the antitumor efficacy of circILNb (Figure S12C). To test whether the therapeutic effect of circILNb depend primarily on pre-existing TILs or peripheral lymphocytes, mice were administered FTY720 to block lymphocyte trafficking from peripheral lymphoid tissues into the tumor. FTY720 treatment did not alter the antitumor effect of circILNb, confirming that its efficacy depended on pre-existing i.t. CD8+ T and NK cells (Figure S12D).

Further functional assays revealed that, CD8+ T cells exhibited an increase in Ki67+ expression following circILNb treatment (Figure 3D). circILNb treatment significantly increased the expression of both IFN-γ and granzyme B in CD8+ cells, while a moderate enhancement was observed in the circIL and circNb treatment groups (Figures 3E and 3F). Moreover, circILNb demonstrated a notable capacity to expand Ki67+ NK cells (Figure 3G). Both circIL and circILNb were capable of markedly elevating the expression of IFN-γ and granzyme B in NK cells (Figures 3H and 3I). Consistently, a significantly higher level of IFN-γ and granzyme B was observed in the treated group compared to the untreated group (Figures S13A and S13B). To determine whether IFN-γ contributes to circILNb-mediated antitumor effect, we treated B16F10 tumor bearing mice with IFN-γ neutralizing antibody during circILNb treatment, and an abrogated antitumor effect was observed (Figure S13C). Together, CD8+ T cells and NK cells contributed to the tumor control and IFN-γ played an essential role in antitumor immunity.

The subsequent investigation focused on the CD8+ T cell memory phenotypes. Within the tumor, the proportion of central memory (Tcm) cells decreased following treatment with circIL and circILNb, whereas the proportion of effector memory (Tem) cells was upregulated (Figures S14A–S14C). Typically, we have observed a significant expansion of tissue-resident memory (Trm) cells following treatment with circIL and circILNb (Figures S14D and S14E). Therefore, circILNb induced effector-type differentiation of CD8+ T cells in the tumor.

To further evaluate the effects of circILNb on i.t. immune responses, we performed an RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis of the TILs sorted from B16F10-OVA tumors treated with or without circILNb. These TILs from mice treated with circILNb exhibited higher expression levels of genes representing T cell activation and cytotoxic function (Figure 3J). Additionally, further quantitative detection of TILs mRNA confirmed significant upregulation of Tbx21, Tnf, and Xcl1 expression following circILNb treatment (Figure 3K). Altogether, circILNb treatment reinvigorated TILs with enhanced activation and toxicity.

sec.title: circILNb expands CD8+ T cells that egress through the tdLN
sec.p: It has been established that DCs that present antigens to the tdLN are capable of delivering i.t. LNP-encapsulated mRNA.29,30 In this study, we examined circNb and circILNb, which have the capacity to express Nb with an HAtag, and found that DCs in the tdLN express Nb (Figure S15A). However, no significant proliferation of DCs in the tdLN was observed after i.t. injection of circILNb (Figure S15B). Meanwhile the maturation of DCs was promoted by circNb or circILNb treatment (Figures S15C and S15D). Given that DC-T cell interactions represent a critical process in tumor immunity, we conducted an in vitro DC-T cell co-culture experiment. This revealed that circILNb enhances the capacity of DCs to activate CD8+ T cell proliferation (Figures S15E and S15F). Collectively, i.t. circILNb-loaded DCs migrated to tdLN where it potentiates CD8+ T cells functional capacity.

Sustained STAT5 activation has been shown to rewire exhausted T cells into an effector profile.31 Probing the STAT5 signaling dynamics in the tdLN 24 h after i.t. dosing with circIL and circILNb revealed robust STAT5 phosphorylation induction of CD8+ T cells (Figures 4A and 4B). This phenomenon prompted us to further explore phenotypic changes in CD8+ T cells within either the tdLN or the tumor (Figure 4C). There was a significant enhancement in the proliferative capacity of tetramer+ CD8+ T cells following circILNb therapy (Figure 4D). Treatment with circIL and circILNb alone resulted in significant expansion of tetramer+ CD8+ T cells (Figure 4E). Moreover, circILNb significant upregulated the differentiation of tdLN-derived tumor-specific memory cells (Ttsm) (Figure 4F). In the tumor, circILNb stimulated CD8+ T cells adopt a stem-like exhausted (Tsle) cells phenotype that possessed key antitumor capabilities (Figure 4G).32,33 Remarkably, circILNb treatment induced the expansion of tetramer+ CD8+ T cells within the tumor, and resulting in a significant increase in the numbers of IFN-γ+ and granzyme B+ CD8+ T cells (Figures 4H–4J). This section demonstrates that circILNb was able to reprogram tumor-specific CD8+ T cells in tdLN and tumor.

sec.title: Local administration of circILNb extends CD8+ T to inhibit tumor growth at distal sites
sec.p: We hypothesized that local administration may elicit a systemic antitumor response. The mice bearing bilateral B16F10 tumors was utilized to assess the effects of circILNb on the untreated tumor (Figure 5A). Strikingly, the administration of circILNb led to the rejection of untreated tumors and protects the mice, resulting in long-term survival (Figures 5B and 5C). To assess the efficacy of the anti-metastatic potential, the B16F10-bearing mice were intravenously injected with B16F10 cells. Fourteen days after injection, the lungs were extracted and the number of metastatic nodules was quantified (Figure 5D). Interestingly, the suppression of growth of lung pseudometastatic foci was achieved through the treatment of circILNb (Figures 5E and 5F). The aforementioned results indicated that the local treatment with circILNb may contribute to a distant antitumor response.

sec.p: Unraveling the mechanistic basis for distant tumor regression following local circILNb treatment represented a critical research priority. Depletion of CD8+ T cells but not NK cells abolished circILNb-induced regression of untreated tumors (Figure S16A). Indeed, circILNb upregulated the proportion of tetramer+ CD8+ T cells in untreated tumor or metastasized lung (Figures S16B and S16C). Notably, FTY720-mediated lymphocyte sequestration abrogated above abscopal effect (Figure S16D). Further mechanistic investigation revealed no detectable upregulation of IL-15 or Nb+ cells in untreated tumors (Figure S16E and S16F). Therefore, peripheral CD8+ T cells played key role in circILNb-induced regression of distant tumors.

It was found that a substantial portion of tetramer+ CD8+ T cells are present in peripheral blood system after circILNb treatment (Figure 5G). Moreover, the proportion of short-lived effector (Tse) increased significantly. Although the proportion of memory precursor effector T (Tmpe) markedly decreased, the proportion of double-positive effector (Tdpe) was increased by circILNb treatment (Figures 5H and 5I). Thus, i.t. injection of circILNb can alter the effector differentiation phenotype of peripheral CD8+ T cells.

sec.title: circILNb emerges better anti-tumor advantage than N-803 plus αPD-L1 or N-809
sec.p: In order to demonstrate the advantages of circILNb, we compared it to the clinically used drug N-803 (Figure 6A). In B16F10, 4T1, and CT26 models, the administration of N-803 plus αPD-L1 had mildly effect on tumor growth or mouse survival (Figures 6B and 6C, 6H, 6I, 6K, and 6L). Worse still, this administration resulted in a significant decrease in mouse body weight in all modals (Figures 6D, 6G, 6J, and 6M). Interestingly, in the RM-1 tumor model, we have observed a comparable antitumor effect between circILNb and the i.t. administration of N-803 in combination with αPD-L1 (Figures 6E and 6F). Therefore, circILNb demonstrated superior efficacy in inhibiting tumor growth, prolonging mouse survival, and exhibiting reduced systemic distress, regardless of whether N-803 and αPD-L1 are administered intratumorally or not. Additionally, we also conducted comparative evaluations against N-809 from preclinical studies, an innovative antibody-drug conjugate fusing N-803 with PD-L1 binding domain (Figure S17A).34 In B16F10 modal, the administration of N-809 had mildly effect on tumor growth or mouse survival, but circILNb demonstrated significantly superior efficacy (Figures S17B and S17C). Interestingly, intratumorally administered circILNb and N-809 yielded comparable effects in the RM-1 model, whereas subcutaneously administered N-809 remained inferior to i.t. injection (Figures S17E and S17F). Subcutaneously administered N-809 exhibited negligible tumor suppression and survival prolongation in 4T1 and CT26 models (Figures S17H, S17I, S17K, and S17L). Notably, attributed to its targeting capability, N-809 exhibited significantly reduced systemic toxicity (Figures S17D, S17G, S17J, and S17M). Therefore, circILNb retained advantages over protein-based therapeutics.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: circRNA has numerous advantages that have not yet been achieved by linear mRNA, such as high stability, prolonged half-life, and economical production. The inherent capacity of circRNA for in situ protein encoding confers potential as an alternative to therapeutic proteins, particularly for small molecular proteins characterized by high synthesis/storage costs and short in vivo half-lives. In this study, we developed the circCV-B3 vector and BAPS method to engineer scarless circRNA with higher circularization efficiency, enhanced encoding capacity, lower immunogenicity, and high purify. Based on the circCV-B3 vector, we designed circILNb that co-encoded the IL-15 and anti-PD-L1 Nb. circILNb effectively suppresses local tumor growth with superior efficacy compared to conventional protein-based therapeutics, indicating the superiority of circRNA-mediated in situ-encoded drug platforms.

circCV-B3 was designed based on the PIE system, an autocatalytic ribozyme characterized by the simplicity and speed of the reaction, the low cost, the suitability for longer sequences, and the non-contamination of proteins.26 Approaches for generating scarless circRNA have been reported in the literatures. For example, T4 RNA ligase has low synthetic efficiency and high cost that limit their application, although the scarless circRNA synthesized by this method are indeed less immunogenic than those synthesized by the PIE method.20 Emerging group II intron-based circularization strategies exhibit high circularization efficiency.35 However, this approach necessitates modifications to the intron sequence according to different CDS, limiting its utility as a versatile protein expression vector. Furthermore, to enhance circularization efficiency, the incorporation of spacer sequences is required, inevitably increasing the length of the circRNA and introducing non-functional elements. In contrast, circCV-B3 does not require sequence alterations based on the CDS and achieves high circularization efficiency without the addition of spacers. Given these points, circCV-B3, with high circularization efficiency (90%) and inheriting the advantages of the PIE system, can serve as a vector for the insertion of any CDSs according to medical application purposes, aiming to minimize synthesis and design costs and providing a convenient platform for the translational application of circRNA.

High purity of circRNA is the basis for high stability of circRNA.26 HPLC relies on the molecular weight difference between the molecules, whereas RNase R unable to degrade linear RNA properly, e.g., G-rich forming G-quadruplexes with intricate secondary structures and need of at least a 7-nucleotide single-stranded 3′ overhang.22,36 Many purification methods have been reported, such as agarose gel electrophoresis separation, introduction of ployA in circRNA, and affinity chromatography, etc., but the high costliness, low efficiency, and complicated process still fail to achieve high purity of circRNA.37,38 In our study, we believe that the contiguous sequence at the junction site is the only sequence present in circRNA, and RNA pull-down targeting this sequence may be the most optimal way to improve circRNA purity. Based on BAPS and the current mature magnetic bead-probe mRNA extraction technique, we found that the probe targeting the junction site could specifically pull down circRNA, and the products showed extremely high purity. However, we encounter many obstacles. Firstly, the denaturing desaturation of circRNA is vitally important, which is directly related to the exposure of the junction site.39 Secondly, the probe design needs to be further optimized, as GC content, length, and quantity all have an impact on hybridization.40 Thirdly, the annealing conditions of circRNA and probe are difficult to control. High binding stability inhibits the dissociation of circRNA, whereas low binding stability reduces the extraction efficiency by washing away most circRNA during contaminant cleaning.41 Fourthly, the steric hindrance posed by circRNA will hinder the binding of the probe to the beads. Therefore, increasing the amount of beads can achieve high-throughput purification of circRNA without reliance on large-scale equipment. Overall, the BAPS method is immature, but it is worth further research and optimization due to its high purification efficiency, low cost, and large-throughput purification.

IL-2 is approved by FDA for metastatic renal cell cancer and advanced melanoma.42 However, IL-2 could induce activation-induced cell death (AICD) and the activation of immune inhibitory Treg cells.43 Moreover, adversely, excessive IL-2 in tumor microenvironment (TME) could also lead to T cell exhaustion and weak responsiveness to ICI therapy.44 Conversely, IL-15 does not induce CD8+ T cell exhaustion, AICD, or Treg cells activation.45 IL-15 exhibits unique properties distinguished from other ICs by providing prolonged signaling for memory differentiation of T cells.46 Mechanistically, IL-15 must be presented by its specific receptor IL-15Rα to bind to its co-activation of receptors IL-15Rβ/γ, which are shared with other IC such as IL-2 and IL-4. Thus, numerous preclinical studies have adopted the IL-15Rα receptor-IL-15 fused form as anticancer therapeutics.9,34,47,48 Moreover, IL-15 can increase PD-L1 expression, indicating its potential to convert cold tumors to hot and making it an optimal partner for ICI.49,50

Protein engineering technologies enable the application of IC and ICI. It is reported that N-803 (IL-15 superagonist), in combination with anti-PD-L1 therapy, achieves enhanced immune activation and antitumor efficacy.50 However, there still exist off-target adverse reactions such as cytokine sink.51,52 On this foundation, N-809, a bifunctional molecule fusing IL-15 with anti-PD-L1, achieves low toxicity.34 However, the impairment of IL-15 activity following fusion to the anti-PD-L1 domain in N-809 may cause the decline in therapeutic effect. Differently, circILNb in this study encoded independent IL-15 and anti-PD-L1 Nb protein without structural interference. Furthermore, attributed to the prolonged expression capacity of circILNb, the tumor retention capability of LNP-encapsulated circILNb and the exceptional tissue penetration of Nb, circILNb exhibited superior suppression of advanced tumors relative to both protein-based therapeutics. Moreover, LNP achieved circILNb retention within tumor, thereby endowing exceptional safety profile.30,53,54 Consequently, the integration of LNP with circRNA via microfluidic technology constitutes a pivotal technological strategy for achieving sustained in situ protein encoding, thereby generating superior therapeutic efficacy relative to protein-based therapeutics.

A notable advantage of tumor-localized immunotherapies is their capacity to eliminate lesions that are not directly treatment. It is evident that CD8+ T cells in the tdLN are educated by DCs that carry tumor antigens and are primed to infiltrate tumor lesions.55 Thus the migration of DCs to tdLN plays a crucial role in regulating systemic tumor progression. Reportedly, i.t. DC internalize LNP-encapsulated mRNA, functioning as carriers to facilitate mRNA transport toward tdLN.29,30,56,57 In this study, activation of DC was observed. Owing to elevated PD-L1 expression and IL-15 secretion in mature DCs, circILNb-loaded DCs is optimally positioned to activate CD8+ T cells within tdLN.58,59,60 This has preliminarily proposed a potential mechanism for intratumorally injected circILNb to elicit systemic immunity.

Previous studies have reported the specific role of IL-15 in promoting the memory differentiation of CD8+ T cells.48,58 In contrast to Tcm cells and Tem cells, Trm cells have been observed to persist within the tumor, where they fulfill a pivotal function in local immunosurveillance.61,62 Our findings indicated that circILNb promoted i.t. Trm cell differentiation. Moreover, it has been reported that Ttsm in the tdLN play a critical role as a source of effector cell generation. These stem-like T cells are primary responders to PD-1/PD-L1 ICB.63 circILNb-loaded DCs may play the key role in Ttsm development. Periphery Tem cells can be classified into at least three distinct subsets: long-lived Tmpe cells, short-lived effector Tse cells, and the double-positive effector Tdpe cells, which possess the capacity to differentiate into exKLRG1 Tem cells.64,65 In this context, our findings indicated that circILNb can upregulated the proportion of periphery Tdpe cells. Given these points, circILNb-loaded cells in tumor stimulate the differentiation of Tem or Trm, and circILNb-loaded DCs migrate to tdLN to elicit robust systemic antitumor memory immune responses.

sec.title: Limitations of the study
sec.p: In this study, the capability of the circCV-B3 vector to engineer circRNA with extended CDS remains unverified. Additionally, the encoding capacity of circILNb remains to be determined, further validation of the yield of IL-15 and anti-PD-L1 Nb would enable a better elucidation of the protein-replacement capacity of circILNb. Regarding the detailed mechanism of circILNb, creating IL-15Rα knockout mice with specific deletions in T cells, NK cells, and DCs and further analysis of tumor or tdLN with single-cell RNA-seq method could provide deeper mechanistic insights into circILNb function in tumor immunity.

sec.title: Experimental model and study participant details
Cell lines
sec.p: HEK293T, A549, B16F10, CT26, RM-1, 4T1, B16F10-OVA cells were cultured in DMEM or RPMI 1640 complete medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, and 1% penicillin-streptomycin solution. Cell culture was undertaken in a CO2 incubator at 37°C. All cell lines were used within 15 passages post-thaw, with identity verified by short tandem repeat and biweekly using Mycoplasma test kit.

sec.title: Mice
sec.p: The female C57BL/6J and BALB/c mice (6- to 8-week-old) were housed under SPF-grade conditions, a temperature-controlled environment on a 12-h light cycle with free access to food and sterile water in the animal facility of Army Medical University. All the animal experiments strictly adhered to the compliance standards of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. The sample sizes were not predetermined using statistical methods; however, they are analogous to those reported in previous publications.66 The collection and analysis of data were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

sec.title: Vector cloning
sec.p: T4td group I introns, CVB3 IRES fragments and RES sequences were chemically synthesized (Sangon Biotech Co., Ltd.) and cloned into a pGEM-T easy plasmid vector containing a T7 RNA polymerase promoter. For circRNA engineering, CDS was either chemically synthesized or PCR amplification from commercial vectors using Cusa Fast Pfu DNA Polymerase (CSB005A, CUSABIO, https://www.cusabio.com/). All CDS was cloned into the RES of circCV-B3 vector using DNA Ligation Kit.

sec.title: circRNA synthesis
sec.p: The production of circRNAs was performed according to previous reports.26 In brief, linear RNA precursors were synthesized via In Vitro Transcription (IVT) from linearized plasmid templates using the T7 High Yield RNA Transcription Kit. Following IVT, the RNA products were treated with DNase I for 15 min to remove the DNA templates. The RNA products were subsequently purified using column purification Kit (Shandong Sparkjade Biotechnology Co., Ltd., AC1704). Subsequently, GTP (2 mM) and MgCl2+ buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT, pH 7.5) were added to the reaction and incubated at 55°C for 15min to promote circularization. Following this step, the synthesized RNA was subjected to a subsequent column purification process.

sec.title: circRNA purification
sec.p: For RNase R + HPLC purification, the synthesized RNA products were heated at 65°C for 5 min and then cooled on ice. The RNA was then treated with RNase R at 37°C for 30 min to enrich circRNAs. RNase R-digested RNA was column-purified. After RNase R treatment, RNA was passed through a 7.8 × 300 mm, 5μm, 1000 Å chromatography column on an HPLC (Waters Arc HPLC). RNA was run in RNase-free buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, pH 6) at a flow rate of 0.3 mL/min. RNA was detected by UV absorbance at 260 nm. The resulting RNA fractions were precipitated with 5 M ammonium acetate, resuspended in water. For BAPS, the protocol has been mentioned (Figure S2B). Briefly, the probes were designed with biotin moieties attached to the ends and stored at 4°C. The RNA product was mixed with the probes in binding buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, 1.0 M LiCl, and 2 mM EDTA, pH 7.5) at 65°C for 5 min, followed by cooling on ice. After rewarming at room temperature, the product was shaken and spun for 2 h. The beads were washed with wash buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, 0.15 M LiCl, and 1 mM EDTA pH 7.5) and was precipitated with a magnetic stand. The beads were then mixed with the RNA-probe complex, and were shaken and spun at room temperature for 15 min. To pull down the circRNA, the beads were washed 5 times in wash buffer preheated at 55°C to remove contaminants, and then is diluted in RNase-free water at 65°C for 5 min. The RNA sample was analyzed by CE5200 (Agilent). The 15nt RNA standard was employed as a positive control. Before the evaluation, the 20ug RNA sample was heated at 65°C for pre-treatment, and then placed on ice and analyzed according to the instrument operating instructions (Prerun: 8.0 KV, 30 s; Sample injection: 5.0 KV, 4 s; Separation: 5.0 KV, 70 min).

sec.title: Urea-agarose gel analysis
sec.p: For the preparation of 6M–1.5% urea–agarose gels, agarose was initially boiled in DEPC-treated H2O, mixed with urea and then topped up with DEPC H2O and 10× TBE to achieve a final 1× TBE concentration. The gels were prepared with 1.5 mm spacers and left at 4°C for gelation for at least 4 h. For loading of RNA samples, 500 ng sample was first denatured in urea loading buffer at 95°C for 2 min and was stained with Safe Red Dye, and then loaded onto each gel. Electrophoreses were operated in a vertical system (Bio-Rad). Gels were run at room temperature at 20 W for 30 min.

sec.title: Lipid nanoparticle encapsulation and characterization
sec.p: LNP-encapsulated circRNA was prepared by microfluidic technology. Briefly, the circRNA was dissolved in citrate buffer (100 mM, pH 4.0) as water phase. The lipid mixtures were dissolved in anhydrous ethanol as the ethanol phase at a molar ratio of 50:10:38.5:1.5 for ionizable lipids (SM-102), 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DSPC), cholesterol and DMG-PEG2000. Then, the ethanol and water phases were then mixed in a microfluidic device at a volume ratio of 1:3 and a flow rate of 12 mL/min. The LNP-circRNA formulations were diluted with a 25-fold volume of 1 × PBS buffer (pH 7.4), and then concentrated with 10 kD Amicon Ultra Centrifugal Filters. Finally, the LNP-circRNA formulations were sterilized with a 0.22 μm filter and stored at 4°C until use. The particle size distribution of the LNPs was ascertained via dynamic light scattering, as measured with a Zetasizer Nano ZS apparatus (Malvern Panalytical). The encapsulation efficiency of circRNA was evaluated by agarose gel electrophoresis. Briefly, for comparison, LNP-encapsulated circRNA is undetectable due to the inability of the nucleic acid probe to penetrate the LNP. However, LNP-encapsulated circRNA was digested by Triton X-100 (2%) to release the internal nucleic acid. The quantification of circRNA was performed using the Quant-iT RiboGreen RNA Assay Kit. The standard curve of circRNA was prepared by continuous dilution from 0 to 2000 ng/mL. Triton X-100 was diluted to 2% with 1 × TE, 100 μL was added to a 96-well black plate, 1 μL of LNP-encapsulated circRNA was added, and it was treated for 5 min, then 100 μL of 200-fold diluted Quant-iT RiboGreen Reagent was added. Similarly, 100 μL of 1 × TE was added to a 96-well black plate. Then 1 μL of LNP-encapsulated circRNA was added, the mixture thoroughly mixed, and 100 μL of 2000-fold diluted Quant-iT RiboGreen Reagent was added. The sample fluorescence was subsequently measured using a fluorescence microplate reader, with standard fluorescein wavelengths set at excitation 480 nm and emission 520 nm. The encapsulation efficiency (in percentage) was calculated as (1 − (non-lysed LNPs/lysed LNPs)) × 100.

sec.title: In vitro expression and immunogenicity analysis
sec.p: A549 cells were seeded in 96-well plates. For each well, 100 ng or equimolar amounts of purified RNAs were transfected. After 24h, the medium was replaced with complete medium. For in vitro detection of luciferase activity, cell lysates were harvested and luciferase activity was measured using the Dual-Luciferase Assay System. For in vitro cell viability analysis, RNA-transfected cells were seeded in a 96 well plate and incubated continuously. CCK-8 was added to the cells and incubated continuously. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm.

sec.title: Tumor inoculation
sec.p: All mice were acclimated for at least 3 days before tumor cell implantation. Tumor cells were implanted as described below, and mouse body weight and tumor volume were monitored at least twice weekly until the experimental endpoints were reached. Tumors were measured using a digital caliper, and volumes were calculated as a2 × b/2, where a < b. Treatments were initiated by random grouping when the tumor reached 150 mm3 to ensure equal mean initial tumor size across groups. Importantly, mice were euthanized when the tumor area exceeded 200 mm3 before therapeutic experiments. The maximal tumor burden was not exceeded in any study in this work. For the survival curve, mice were sacrificed when a or b of the tumor was larger than 1.5 cm each, the tumor volume exceeded 1500 mm3 or the body weight decreased by more than 20% of the treatment-onset body weight. For single tumor experiments, mice were injected subcutaneously in the shaved right flank with B16F10 or B16F10-OVA (1 × 106), CT26 (0.5 × 106) and RM-1 (0.5 × 106) in a volume of 50 μL of PBS. 4T1 (1 × 106) in a volume of 50 μL of PBS was orthotopically implanted into the left mammary fat pad of female BALB/c mice. For double tumor experiments, the contralateral tumor was injected with 0.5 × 106 B16F10-OVA cells in a volume of 50 μL of PBS on the left flank after inoculation of the primary right tumor. To simulate a more malignant invasion and hematogenous metastasis. 0.2 × 106 B16F10-OVA cells in 100 μL of PBS were inoculated retro-orbitally after the primary flank tumor was established. Fifteen days after surgery, fresh lungs were harvested from euthanized mice and metastatic nodules were quantified.

sec.title: Primary CD8+ T and natural killer cells preparation
sec.p: Spleens from 6- to 8-week-old C57BL/6J female mice were harvested and processed into single-cell suspensions. Erythrocytes were lysed using ACK lysis buffer. CD8+ T cells were isolated using the Mouse CD8+ T cell isolation kit (UElandy, Suzhou, China, M7402). NK cells were isolated using the EasySort Mouse NK Cell Isolation Kit (Elabscience BiotechnologyCo.,Ltd., MIM005N). All isolated cells resuspended at a concentration of 106 cells/ml in complete RPMI medium. Isolated CD8+ T cells were additionally supplemented with 10 ng/mL of murine IL-2 and were activated for 48 h on nontissue culture-treated plate that was precoated with 0.5 μg/mL of anti-CD3 and 5 μg/mL of anti-CD28 overnight at 4°C. After activation, T cells were cultured for 48 h before use in downstream experiments.

sec.title: In vitro phosphorylated STAT5 experiments
sec.p: Primary CD8+ T cells (starved of IL-2 for 24 h) and NK cells were seeded into 96-well plates at 10,000 cells per well. 100ng of circIL or circILnR were transfected for 12 h and subsequently washed twice before resting for 24h with anti-IL-15Rα neutralization antibody. Cells were immediately conducted for p-STAT5 assay.

sec.title: In vitro T cell proliferation assay
sec.p: For bone marrow dendritic cells (BMDCs) preparation, a 1 mL syringe was used to gently flush the femur and tibia to release the bone marrow into PBS. The flushing and aspiration were repeated until no visible clumps of bone marrow tissue remained. The suspension was then centrifuged at 500 g for 5 min to collect the cells. Erythrocytes were lysed using ACK lysis buffer. cells resuspended at a concentration of 106 cells in 15 mL of complete RPMI medium supplemented with 5 ng/mL of GM-CSF and IL-4 and seeded in a 100 mm Petri dish for 6 days in incubator. Half of the culture medium was replaced with complete RPMI supplemented with 5 ng/mL of IL-4 and GM-CSF every alternate day. For the T cell proliferation assay. The 5 x 103 BMDCs were pulsed for 5 h with 10 ng/mL OVA257-264 (SIINFEKL) peptides. Then cells were washed twice with PBS and were transfected with 50 ng circLuc or circILNb, and subsequently co-cultured with CFSE-labelled stimulated CD8+ T cells at a ratio of 1:10 for 48 h. T cell proliferation was evaluated by measuring the dilution of CFSE using flow cytometry. The decrease in fluorescence intensity of CFSE in T cells served as an indicator of their proliferation.

sec.title: In vivo drug administration
sec.p: CircScram (circLuc), circIL, circNb and circILNb were administered by i.t. injection. Mice were anesthetized with 2.5% isoflurane, and 50 μL of PBS or LNP-encapsulated circRNA was injected intratumorally into the tumor every 5 days unless otherwise noted. For immune cell depletion studies, B16F10 or B16F10-OVA tumor-bearing mice were injected intravenously with IgG control. Immune cell depletion was initiated 1 day prior to treatment and was performed with antibodies against CD8, NK1.1, CD4. All depletions were administered i.p. 200 μg before treatment initiation and every 3 days for the remaining days. To study the effect of lymphocytes egressing from lymph nodes, tumor-bearing mice (>12 days) were intraperitoneally administered with 1 mg/kg FTY720 starting on the day before circRNA treatment initiation and then 0.5mg/kg administered every other day. For comparison with protein therapy, advanced tumor-bearing mice (about 150 mm3) were treated with 10 mg/kg α-PD-L1 (i.p./i.t.) (BioXCell, BE0101), 200 μg/kg N-803 (Inbakicept) (s.c./i.t.) or 2 mg/kg N-809 (s.c./i.t.) which was synthesized by GenScript.

sec.title: In vitro Nb blocking assays
sec.p: B16F10 PD-L1+ cells were pre-stimulated 24 h with 20 ng/mL IFN-γ. For Nb blocking assays, the amount of Nb was normalized according to the detection in the supernatant by Western blot analysis (quantification was performed by ImageJ). B16F10 PD-L1+ cells were first incubated with either supernatants from circNbs-transfected HEK293T cells, PD-L1 specific mAb or control medium. Cells were then washed and stained with recombinant PD-1-PE obtained by coupling recombinant mouse PD-1 Fc chimera to R-phycoerythrin using Lightning-Link R-PE Labeling Kit. The percentage of rPD-1 blocking activity was calculated as [1-(rPD-1 median PE fluorescence intensity with circNbs treated samples/mean rPD-1 median PE fluorescence intensity with medium-treated samples)]x100.

sec.title: Cell preparation and flow cytometry analysis
sec.p: B16F10-OVA tumors or lungs from the metastatic melanoma model were harvested, weighed and then minced using dissection scissors. As noted in the manufacturer protocol, tissues were digested with 1 mg/mL collagenase I and 0.5 mg/mL DNase I in RPMI containing 25 mM HEPES for 50 min at 37°C with shaking. The cell suspension was then passed through a 70 μm MACS SmartStrainer to remove undigested tissue and then resuspended in PBS at 106 cells/ml. Equal volumes of samples were separated using Percoll solution to separate TILs. For tdLN or blood, tdLN was harvested, weighed and then dissociated and filtered through a 70 μm cell strainer. Blood was collected by the retro-orbital route into tubes and erythrocytes were lysed using ACK lysis buffer. All cell samples were washed twice with PBS at 106 cells/ml. For performing intracellular staining, cells were fixed and permeabilized using the Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set. Intracellular staining was performed with antibodies diluted in permeabilization buffer. Intracellular cytokine staining was performed using the Cytofix/Cytoperm Fixation/Permeabilization Kit and Brefeldin A. Subsequent washes and surface staining were resuspended in Mouse Fc block Plus (BioLegend, 101301) before surface staining for 15 min to block non-specific binding and then stained with conjugated antibodies in cell staining buffer. For in vivo analysis of STAT5 phosphorylation, tdLN was mechanically disrupted on a cell strainer directly in the lyse/fix buffer (BD Biosciences, 558049) to produce single-cell suspensions. After washed, and fixed with BD Phosflow Fixation Buffer I pre-warmed to 37°C for 10 min and permeabilized with BD Phosflow Perm Buffer III pre-chilled to −20°C for 30 min on ice, cells were subsequently stained for 1 h at RT with antibodies in PBS (1:1,000 dilution) for 30 min at room temperature. Undetected cells were washed with flow buffer, fixed in 1% formalin, and stored at 4°C until flow cytometric analysis. Cells were harvested using a BD FAC-Symphony A1 or LSR Fortessa instrument (BD Biosciences) with FACSDiva software.

sec.title: In vivo bioimaging
sec.p: Luciferase signals were analyzed by in vivo bioluminescence imaging (BLI) using the NEWTON 7.0 IVIS Spectrum Imaging System (Vilber Bio Imaging). Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane gas (2% isoflurane in oxygen, 1 L/min) during injection and imaging procedures. Intraperitoneal injections of 150 mg/kg D-Luciferin provide a saturating substrate concentration for the Fluc enzyme. Mice were imaged in a light-tight chamber using an in vivo optical imaging system equipped with a cooled charge-coupled device camera. During imaging, mice inhaled isoflurane delivered via a nose cone, and their body temperature was maintained at 37C in the dark box of the camera system. Bioluminescence images were acquired between 10 and 20 min after luciferin administration. Mice usually recovered from anesthesia within 2 min of imaging. To examine the anatomic location of circRNA translation, mice bearing B16F10 tumors received a single i.t. injection of circLuc, tumor, heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney and representative tdLN and non-tdLN were harvested after 24h, and luciferase expression was assessed ex vivo. Tissues were imaged 15 min after incubation with 150 μg/mL D-luciferin.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence
sec.p: Frozen tumor samples from circNb- or circILNb-treated mice were sectioned at 6 μm using cryostat. Sections were thawed and immediately fixed in 4% formaldehyde for 5 min. All the following steps were performed at room temperature. Endogenous peroxidases were blocked with IHC/ISG Peroxidase Block (Jackson, ENZ-ACC107-0100) for 15 min. Protein blocking was performed with a solution of TBS-Tween containing 2% milk, 5% biotin-free BSA and 1% human immunoglobulins (Privigen, CSL Behring) for 1h. For sections to be stained with anti-rat IgG-HRP secondary, 1.25% goat serum was added to the mixture (VectorLab, MP-7444). Primary antibodies were diluted in TBS-Tween containing 1% BSA and incubated for 1h at room temperature. Rabbit anti-HA tag antibody was used to detect the Nb. Rabbit PD-L1 specific antibody was used to detect PD-L1. These primary antibodies were followed by anti-rabbit IgG (Cell Signaling Technologies, 4412S) or anti-rat IgG (Cell signaling, 4417S). Images were captured using Oyster PANNORAMIC 250 Flash III (3DHISTECH).

sec.title: RNA sequencing analysis
sec.p: TILs were isolated from B16F10-OVA tumor–bearing mice 24 h after the second injection of circILNb. Total RNA extraction, cDNA library construction, sequencing, and data analysis were performed by the Wuhan Metware Technology Co., Ltd. using the Metware cloud platform. Raw counts that fell on exons of each gene were calculated and normalized to obtain RPKM (Reads Per Kilobase per Million mapped reads) values. The FPKM of these genes were logarithmically (fold-change) converted.

sec.title: Cytokines ELISA assay
sec.p: The isolated serum samples were then stored at −20°C. The mass density of the serum was taken as 1 g/mL for conversion. All mouse sera were heat-inactivated at 56°C for 35 min before use. For the analysis of i.t. IFN-γ and granzyme B secretion levels, weighted tumor tissue harvested from tumor-bearing mice was homogenized in PBS at 4°C. The sample was centrifuged and the supernatant was collected to equilibrate total protein using a BCA kit. All cytokine concentrations were calculated from a standard curve generated with known amounts.

sec.title: Western blot
sec.p: Culture medium from transfected HEK293T cells was collected, centrifuged to pellet cell debris, and the supernatant was ultrafiltration (Merck millipore, UFC800396). Protein concentration was evaluated by BCA protein assay. Samples were then added with Pierce Lane Marker Reducing Sample Buffer (ThermoFisher, 39000), heated (95°C, 10min) and loaded onto polyacrylamide gels (15%) (Shandong Sparkjade Biotechnology Co., Ltd., EC0025-B). After migration, proteins were transferred to PVDF stacks. The membrane was blocked with 5% milk and stained with anti-HA tag or anti-IL-15. HRP-conjugated anti-mouse IgG (Sigma-Aldrich, RABHRP2) or HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG (Sigma-Aldrich, RABHRP1) were used as secondary antibodies. Protein detection was performed using the Hypersensitive ECL substrate. Images were captured using a Fusion FX camera (Vilbert Lourmat).

sec.title: RT-qPCR
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted using AFTSpin Cell Fast RNA Extraction Kit. For RT–qPCR, initially, total RNA for each sample was reverse transcribed. Subsequently, the qPCR reaction was carried out using LightCycler 96 instrument (Roche). All samples were normalized to GAPDH expression and calculated using the 2-(DDCt) method.

sec.title: Quantification and statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using Prism 10 (GraphPad Software), and are presented as mean ± s.d. Comparisons between two groups were performed using the paired or unpaired Student’s t test, as indicated. Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to compare tumor growth curves. For survival curves, the log rank test was used. The p values in the figures is indicated unless otherwise stated.
